plain_text:
Music can make you feel better on a bad day, but can it
literally take your pain away? Research suggests that
music—and sound in general—may have the power to do
just that. An international team of scientists, led in part
by investigators from the National Institute of Dental and
Craniofacial Research, studied mice to understand how
this process works. Their findings could open the door to
new, safer ways to treat pain in humans.
semantic_text: Music can make you feel better on a bad day, but can it literally take your pain away? Research suggests that music—and sound in general—may have the power to do just that. An international team of scientists, led in part by investigators from the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research, studied mice to understand how this process works. Their findings could open the door to new, safer ways to treat pain in humans.

plain_text:
Since the 1960s, music and other sounds have been found
to ease pain from a range of different health conditions and
procedures. Research shows that sound can reduce the pain
of dental extractions, sickle cell disease, and childbirth,
among others.
semantic_text: Since the 1960s, music and other sounds have been found to ease pain from a range of different health conditions and procedures. Research shows that sound can reduce the pain of dental extractions, sickle cell disease, and childbirth, among others.

plain_text:
According to Yuanyuan “ Kevin ” Liu, Ph.D., an investigator
for the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial
Research (NIDCR), music can grab our attention and
help us relax. But his team's recent findings suggest the
analgesic (pain-reducing) effect is from sound rather
than music specifically. Dr. Liu studies sensory biology
and pain. He is especially interested in the relationship
between the mind and body and the role that perceptions
play in this relationship.
semantic_text: According to Yuanyuan “ Kevin ” Liu, Ph.D., an investigator for the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR), music can grab our attention and help us relax. But his team's recent findings suggest the analgesic (pain-reducing) effect is from sound rather than music specifically. Dr. Liu studies sensory biology and pain. He is especially interested in the relationship between the mind and body and the role that perceptions play in this relationship.

plain_text:
To find out how sound dulls pain, Dr. Liu and a group
of researchers in the United States and China turned to
unlikely research subjects: mice with inflamed paws.
semantic_text: To find out how sound dulls pain, Dr. Liu and a group of researchers in the United States and China turned to unlikely research subjects: mice with inflamed paws.

plain_text:
For three days in a row, Dr. Liu and his team exposed the
mice to three different sounds:
semantic_text: For three days in a row, Dr. Liu and his team exposed the mice to three different sounds:

plain_text:
■ Harmonious classical music (composed by Bach)
■ Inharmonious music (an unpleasant rearrangement
of the same Bach piece)
■ Background/white noise
semantic_text: ■ Harmonious classical music (composed by Bach) ■ Inharmonious music (an unpleasant rearrangement of the same Bach piece) ■ Background/white noise

plain_text:
The researchers used a technique to measure and compare the
mice's pain sensitivity before and after hearing the sounds.
semantic_text: The researchers used a technique to measure and compare the mice's pain sensitivity before and after hearing the sounds.

plain_text:
All three kinds of sound reduced the mice's pain.
Surprisingly, the harmonious music was no more or less
effective than the other sounds. The sounds also only reduced
pain when played at very low intensities—just above a whisper.
When the intensity increased, these effects disappeared.
semantic_text: All three kinds of sound reduced the mice's pain. Surprisingly, the harmonious music was no more or less effective than the other sounds. The sounds also only reduced pain when played at very low intensities—just above a whisper. When the intensity increased, these effects disappeared.

plain_text:
Dr. Liu explained that it was not the sound's volume itself
but rather the signal-to-noise ratio—the sound's intensity
compared to the background noise. The sweet spot for pain
relief was just above the level of the background noise.
semantic_text: Dr. Liu explained that it was not the sound's volume itself but rather the signal-to-noise ratio—the sound's intensity compared to the background noise. The sweet spot for pain relief was just above the level of the background noise.

plain_text:
Dr. Liu compared this to using background music
played at a low volume, which he does when he needs
to concentrate: “Just a little bit of sound, not too loud.
Maybe that's the magic?”
